title: AI for Production — Module 1: Introduction to LLMs
subject: Automation and language models in production work: two original concept recordings.
audience: Production engineers, supervisors, operations analysts, maintenance teams and manufacturing professionals who are new to AI. Learners understand basic production processes and can read simple tables and reports. Programming experience is not required. Use clear language, manufacturing examples and guided demonstrations.
outcomes: Distinguish fixed automation from AI assistance and explain why factory-specific language-model answers need supporting evidence and verification. This standalone release covers only the two original Module 1 recordings, not the full seven-module course.

objectives.text: Distinguish fixed automation from AI assistance using production-work examples.
Explain how language models generate text and why their outputs require verification.

dependencies: One standalone module. Watch Automation vs AI before What are Large Language Models. Then complete worked examples, guided practice, Scenario Lab and module quiz, followed by one guided evidence-review project, 80% final assessment and reflection.
systemPrompt: Create this standalone Module 1 course from ONLY the two original SCORM Builder recordings and their locally reviewed transcripts. Preserve the two exact objectives and the recordings. Keep all source content local; do not call external AI/transcription services. Generate simple source-linked learning activities and exactly two pre-checkpoint questions per video. Include a module quiz and one guided ready-made in-course project learners run and explain without editing. Finish with an objective-aligned 80% final assessment and reflection. Qualify the recording’s absolute RAG accuracy and local-security claims in visible review notes; no diagnostic or equipment-control instructions. Do not claim this is the seven-module AI for Production course.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of manufacturing operations, production reports and workplace procedures. Familiarity with spreadsheets is helpful. No prior AI or programming knowledge is required.

topics.title: LLM capabilities, limits and factory grounding

instructions.scope: Use only the two supplied original recordings. Teach fixed-rule automation, deterministic responses, changed operating conditions, AI pattern-based adaptation, and the respective roles of machinery, AI and humans. Explain LLM parameters and text-based assistance, basic prompting examples, limitations without factory/current data, and the demonstrated use of retrieved SOPs and live telemetry in a local deployment example. Preserve the two original videos and locally reviewed transcripts.
instructions.exclusions: Do not add recordings or illustrated replacement videos. Do not teach detailed next-token prediction, transformer mechanics, a comprehensive local-versus-cloud comparison or a structured-prompt method: these are not supplied by these two recordings. Course objectives O3 and O4 require later reviewed teaching. No external tools, machine operation, repairs, separate module project or course final assessment.
instructions.prerequisites: Basic production-process and report awareness; no AI or programming background required.
instructions.teachingNotes: Generate a simple fictional problem hook, worked reasoning, guided evidence-review practice, transfer scenarios, exactly two first-half-supported midpoint questions per video, and one module quiz covering O1/O2. Keep all work inside the course and distinguish supplied evidence from unsupported conclusions. The second source overstates RAG accuracy and local security; flag those statements for human SME review, never turn them into guaranteed facts or correct-answer claims. Use clear language, plausible similar-length options and explicit Select one answer / Select all correct answers labels. Original recordings remain unchanged; local transcript review is AI-assisted, not final human source approval.

sources.text:
Step onto the floor of a modern manufacturing plant,

and you'll immediately notice the perfect synchronization.

Every movement is timed down to the millisecond.

For decades, we've built these systems to solve one specific problem,

eliminating repetitive physical labor.

This relies on an environment of known knowns.

If the size, weight, and speed of the materials on the line never fluctuate, the output remains entirely predictable.

You program a programmable logic controller, or PLC, with a set ladder logic sequence, and the machinery executes those exact steps millions of times without deviation.

The result is a consistent execution engine that is completely blind to its surrounding context. The trouble is, a factory floor is a physical space, and physical spaces change.

Bearings wear down, ambient room temperature fluctuates, and supply chains deliver materials

with slightly different dimensions.

This diagram shows what happens to hard-coded logic when an irregular variable enters the

sequence.

The rules don't adapt to the new shape.

The pathway stops and the line halts.

To keep the line moving, engineers must monitor operations, find the new variable,

and manually rewrite the code to account for the change.

We eliminated the physical repetition, but humans are still performing the repetitive

thinking required to manage the machines.

To scale operations efficiently, a facility needs a way to hand off

that cognitive repetition.

It requires artificial intelligence.

Let's look at a specific industrial process,

managing the internal temperature of a single machine.

This chart shows how traditional automation

handles the cooling cycle.

The rule is simple.

If the temperature crosses a hard 70 degrees,

the cooler turns on.

This logic is deterministic.

The machine checks the temperature, returning a strict binary yes or no.

Over a month of operation, the coolant fluid inside the machine ages, losing its

thermal efficiency.

A 70 degree trigger is no longer the most efficient threshold, yet the system will continue waiting for that exact number before activating.

The execution is restricted by the initial parameters set by a human programmer,

which prevents the system from optimizing for real-time wear and tear.

Now, let's apply an artificial intelligence model to that exact same cooling problem.

AI plots thousands of past temperature readings against cooler events

to discover relationships and identify optimal cooling zones.

By recognizing patterns, it manages unknown knowns.

As coolant degrades, the AI adapts, triggering coolers earlier.

This probabilistic approach generates variable confidence scores for actions

based on current conditions rather than binary commands.

Probabilistic systems rely on operational history to weigh options and make informed

decisions on the fly. Zooming out to the entire factory floor, we can see how these two technologies interact.

AI and traditional automation are not competitors.

They occupy different layers in a production hierarchy.

On the floor, the conveyor belts and robotic arms remain in place, handling the heavy,

repetitive physical execution.

Above them, the AI acts as a coordinating layer.

It monitors the entire flow,

predicting when a motor might fail,

or adjusting conveyor speeds to prevent a bottleneck.

A modern facility maximizes its throughput

when adaptive digital intelligence is layered

directly over consistent physical machinery.

This division of labor shifts the daily responsibilities

of the human workforce.

By offloading micro-decisions like when to trigger a valve or how fast a belt should turn

to the AI, technicians are no longer required to spend their shifts manually troubleshooting basic

logic failures. Instead of fixing a single machine's code, a worker now manages the performance

targets for the entire line, adjusting the system's objectives based on production deadlines or material quality.

In modern manufacturing, the roles are distinct.

Automation executes the physical tasks, AI decides how to optimize those tasks, and humans

set the goals that the entire system works toward.

sources.text:
Modern manufacturing relies heavily on constant momentum,

right up until a critical piece of machinery suddenly grinds to a halt.

To get the line moving again, technicians face an immediate bottleneck.

They have to manually dig through mountains of unstructured text,

flipping through hundreds of pages of maintenance manuals

and dense standard operating procedures just to find a starting point.

This search quickly turns into a maze.

An obscure error code on one screen rarely matches the disconnected sensor descriptions

buried deep in a PDF from five years ago.

The actual physical repair often takes minutes.

The true financial bleed of machine downtime comes from the hours wasted simply searching

for the exact information needed to act. This massive data bottleneck is exactly the problem large language models or LLMs

are engineered to solve.

They instantly process and synthesize massive volumes of unstructured human text.

Think of an LLM as an AI trained by reading vast oceans of existing information, everything

from heavy technical manuals to complex

code bases and millions of web pages.

We call them large because of their parameters.

These are billions of mathematical knobs storing patterns and logic the model learned

during training.

This parameter-heavy architecture powers systems dominating the current landscape, including

OpenAI's GPT-4, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and local

alternatives like Meta's Llama 3.

By leveraging these billions of parameters, LLMs act as universal translators, taking a

factory's overwhelming pile of static documentation and turning it into accessible,

interactive knowledge.

Out of the box, an LLM offers immediate industrial utility.

It inherently understands dense technical jargon,

complex error codes, and niche sensor descriptions,

without requiring you to retrain the software

for every new task.

You interact with it through prompting.

You simply type plain language instructions,

asking the system to summarize a manual,

explain a process, or compare technical data,

and it responds in context.

However, these models arrive with a significant structural flaw.

A standard LLM possesses absolutely zero knowledge of your facility's specific proprietary data.

If you ask an ungrounded LLM about a specific, localized machine, it will experience a hallucination, generating a highly plausible sounding, but entirely false answer.

Furthermore, generalized LLMs have no concept of time.

They are completely blind to real-time events, live telemetry, and current machine

statuses.

Deploying a raw, generalized LLM on a factory floor creates a dangerous gap between broad

assumptions and specific real-world truths.

It quickly becomes a profound operational liability.

Safely deploying these models in manufacturing requires a specialized architectural process,

known as retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, combined with live data integration.

The RAG workflow begins when a technician submits a query.

The system first extracts the exact proprietary SOP document

from your secure local database.

Simultaneously, it pulls real time telemetry,

merging it with the SOP into a single context package.

This forces the LLM to answer strictly using local data.

This specific workflow neutralizes the threat

of hallucinations.

It forces the AI to strictly read your proprietary manual and check your live sensors before it is allowed to speak.

Back on the factory floor, our technician is now standing beside the halted machine, actively attempting a diagnosis.

They encounter a highly obscure, completely undocumented error code and input it straight into the tablet's interface. Because this facility runs a local model like Llama 3 via

Ollama, the entire query processes completely on

premises.

The factories telemetry and intellectual property never

leave the building.

Nothing touches the external internet, keeping the

proprietary information perfectly secure.

This secure local processing instantly synthesizes the relevant manual and the live machine status,

delivering a verified step-by-step repair guide directly into the technician's hands.

Large language models arrive with no inherent understanding of a specific business or its unique workflows.

They function as specialized reasoning engines, using mathematical patterns to organize and navigate complex technical text.

This reasoning capability delivers its highest industrial utility when the engine is securely

anchored to a facility's specific proprietary truth.

Mastering this connection makes once scattered factory data a facility's single most accessible

and actionable asset.
